newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Australian Dairy Vale eyes exports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Australian Dairy Vale eyes exports.

text.p: South Australian milk processor Dairy Vale Ltd is trimming its operational fat and looking at shaking up the local dairy product market with a new range of products ahead of plans for a growing push on export markets.

The unlisted public company lifted operational profit after tax in 1995/96 to June 30 by 182 percent to A$2.9 million, chiefly through buoyant exports, but still fell short of a A$5.34 million profit forecast in its January 1995 prospectus.

Dairy Vale has promised further profit improvement in 1996/97 but new managing director Glenn Wheatland warns it will be a tough year for exports with a rising Australian dollar and says domestic strength must be the key to its long-term future.
This week the company launched an assault on the local market with a new range of flavoured milk and iced coffee products, with a new logo, packaging and marketing push.
In an interview this week, Wheatland told Reuters the new range was absolutely vital to the company's future.

It faces formidable competition from National Foods Ltd subsidiary National Dairies which he said had a significant selling advantage for its other products in its 90 percent market share of iced coffee, a big seller in the state.

"My view is that National Dairies have had it their way too long and we are going to give them a bit of a shakeup," Wheatland said. Dairy Vale processes 240 million litres of milk a year, of which 140 million litres goes into cheese, 50-60 million for fresh white and flavoured milk sales and 40 million litres for UHT longlife milk, icecream and yoghurt products.
Wheatland said the company currently achieves 25-30 percent of revenue from exports, chiefly to Asian markets, which he hopes to grow to about 50 percent within the next five years.
However export margins are under pressure and low price competition in cheese is having the same impact domestically.
"It is going to be a tough year," he said.
"One of the things Dairy Vale needed to do was to make sure the domestic base was substantial and very profitable and that is basically what I have been aiming to do," he said.

Dairy Vale, which is 46.2 percent owned by the Dairy Vale Investment Trust and the remainder by farmer suppliers, is seen by food industry analysts as a potential longer-term target for takeover as the fractured industry undergoes rationalisation.
"It is not particularly an easy business, but a very strategic business," one analyst told Reuters, saying Dairy Vale currently sold at a 20 percent discount to asset backing.

Wheatland, who joined the company in January, said Dairy Vale was left behind by deregulation in 1994, being largely unprepared for large cost increases in selling and distribution. He said Dairy Vale was working on a stream of efficiency moves, including rationalising factories, its vendor system and depots, upgrading facilities and selling off its non-core rural supplies stores, although talks fell through recently with prospective buyer IAMA Ltd.

Dairy Vale has stabilised its share of the white milk market in South Australia at 38.5 percent, aided by gaining a state government milk supply contract which, while not big margin, cuts unit costs of production by providing good throughput.

With no net debt, Wheatland said Dairy Vale was looking at a major investment for the export market, setting up plant, at a cost of A$10-15 million, to produce whey powder, a cheese byproduct used in Asia as infant formula and in confectionery.
The company is looking at possible joint venture partners offshore and expects to make a decision this financial year.
"We believe there is a massive market for the product and we are looking at the option that whey powder may be a significant amount of income and profit for (us)," he said.
Longer-term the company is looking at other acquisitions and while Wheatland is coy on targets, he said they were likely to be in food and beverages but not necessarily in milk products.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
